subject: Computer Networking
title: Handoffs Between Towers
description: A quick win: understand Handoffs Between Towers.

hook.text: You're on a call driving at highway speed. You pass five cell towers. The call never drops. How?

buildup.text: Your phone constantly measures signal strength from nearby towers. The network knows when a handoff is needed.

discovery.text: A soft handoff connects you to the new tower before dropping the old one. There's a brief overlap, not a gap.

twist.text: VoLTE calls are especially sensitive. A botched handoff during a voice call is immediately noticeable to the user.

climax.text: 5G networks make handoffs faster and more complex — with small cells, a car might switch towers every few seconds.

punchline.text: Handoffs are invisible when they work. You only notice when they fail.

quiz.question: What is a soft handoff in cellular networks?
options: Connecting to a new tower before disconnecting from the old one
Turning off the phone and reconnecting

details.summary: Handoffs transfer an active call or data session from one cell tower to another as a user moves. The phone continuously measures signal strength from surrounding towers and the network decides when to switch.
details.whyItMatters: Seamless handoffs are what make mobile phone calls and data sessions work while moving. Without them, every time you passed a cell boundary, your connection would drop.
takeaways: Handoffs transfer connections between towers during movement
Soft handoff maintains two connections briefly for no interruption
The network uses signal strength measurements to trigger handoffs

faq.question: What happens during a handoff?
faq.answer: The phone reports signal strength measurements to the network. When the current tower's signal weakens and a neighbor's strengthens, the network initiates a handoff. Data is buffered briefly during the switch.

faq.question: Why do calls sometimes drop during handoffs?
faq.answer: Drops occur when there is no suitable tower to hand off to — coverage gaps, congested towers refusing new connections, or signal changing too quickly for the network to react. Buildings, tunnels, and terrain create dead zones.
